ethiopia.title: Children among 139 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says
ethiopia.content: Djibouti boat capsize: Children among 139 dead with 84 still missing, UN says - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Children among 139 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says Image source, International Organization for Migration Image caption, IOM workers receiving migrants near Guhere, north of the port town of Obock By Hafsa Khalil Published 11 October 2026 At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said. The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said. IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere. Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says. The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered. "This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives." Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them. Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change. Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti. Image caption, The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen IOM said it was providing assistance to 64 of the survivors at its response centre in Obock, including healthcare and support to "restore contact with their families". The UN agency was working in "close collaboration" with local authorities to help migrants and "prevent deaths at sea and on land", it added. More than 900 migrants died or went missing taking the same route in 2025, during an 18% increase in the number of people attempting the journey, according to IOM statistics. In March 2026, nine people were killed and 45 went missing following a similar incident as Thursday's. The conflict in Yemen has also displaced more than 130,000 people across the country, the UN refugee agency said last month. Thousands of Yemenis have fled to Djibouti to escape the civil war between Houthi fighters and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Djibouti is a tiny former French colony that sits just across the Gulf of Aden from Yemen. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops cross border
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops enter Tigray - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Ethiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops cross border Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Ethiopian forces took control of Tigray's main city Mekelle from rebel forces last week By Hafsa Khalil and Kaleb Moges , BBC Africa Published 9 October 2026 Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country. In a letter sent to the UN Security Council and seen by the BBC, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence". Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour. Fighting broke out two weeks ago between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended a civil war. Ethiopia says Eritrea is backing the TPLF, which it denies. During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF. But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week. Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray. Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war. US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight. One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed. Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported. There have so far been no verified reports of casualties. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray. Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity." But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory. On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms". In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition". Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power. This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September. Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control. ethiopia.title: Eritrean troops move deep into Ethiopia's Tigray region, residents tell BBC
ethiopia.content: Tigray conflict: Eritrean troops move deep into Ethiopia, residents tell BBC - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Eritrean troops move deep into Ethiopia's Tigray region, residents tell BBC Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Eritrean soldiers were involved in fighting in Tigray during the 2020-2022 conflict By Yemane Nagish , BBC Tigrinya and Michael Teferi , BBC Africa Published 7 October 2026 Eritrean soldiers have crossed into northern Ethiopia heading towards an area where clashes have been taking place between national army troops and regional forces, residents in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat have told the BBC. Fighting in the region broke out two weeks ago after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). Both blame one another for violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war. Ethiopia has also accused Eritrea of backing the TPLF - something Asmara has previously denied. The latest unrest follows the launch in September of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia, which includes the TPLF. How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia Published 2 October The young women who fought in Ethiopia's last civil war and don't want to see another one Published 6 March Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? Published 28 September Over the weekend, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control. Eritrea was a key ally of landlocked Ethiopia during the 2020-2022 war, fighting against the TPLF in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century and which drove the Tigray region to the precipice of famine. But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports. Last week the two countries severed diplomatic relations as the renewed fighting raised fears of a wider regional conflict. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas, though mobile phone connections and internet access have been restored to most areas since the military took over Mekelle. According to multiple accounts, Eritrean troops have moved from the border town of Zalambessa towards central Tigray, with convoys reportedly passing through Adigrat and heading toward Edaga Hamus, a town between Adigrat and Mekelle. "I saw about 40 trucks carrying soldiers. The convoy was moving south," one resident of Adigrat, who requested anonymity for security reasons, told BBC Tigrinya. Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Pro-government forces have control of Mekelle, the capital of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region A second resident reported seeing troop movements, initially at night: "We have been seeing trucks with Eritrean registration plates passing through the city. "Now this morning we witnessed around 20 to 30 large trucks heading toward Edaga Hamus." He added that acquaintances travelling along the route had seen additional vehicles carrying heavy weapons, including anti-aircraft guns, and noted some troops were also moving on foot. A source in Mekelle told the BBC that relatives in Adigrat described even larger troop movements, and estimated they saw up to 60 trucks carrying soldiers who were later deployed in mountainous terrain near Edaga Hamus. Images circulating on social media appear to show heavily loaded military trucks carrying uniformed personnel towards Adigrat, Edaga Hamus and possibly Wukro, another key town along the corridor between Adigrat and Mekelle. The BBC has not independently verified the images. Sources in Wukro told the BBC that national army soldiers and allied fighters had entered the town on Wednesday after an exchange of heavy weapons about 15km south of the town. The BBC has not yet been able to independently verify any of the reported troop movements. The reported return of Eritrean forces has sparked anxiety among many of Tigray's residents, with some recalling the atrocities allegedly committed by soldiers from Eritrea during the recent civil war , when they fought against the TPLF. One Adigrat resident said that seeing Eritrean soldiers again was emotionally distressing: "The memories are still fresh. I was emotional myself. People are saddened to see them back again." A resident of Edaga Hamus also reported Eritrean troops passing through the town and said drone strikes had occurred nearby, with soldiers targeted. In a recent interview with private station Fana Television, senior Ethiopian government official Abraham Belay accused Eritrea of direct participation in the conflict. "The Eritrean army has participated with its full capacity and logistics," he said. "Many Eritrean soldiers have been killed and captured. There is no doubt that the retaliation will be double. They will see what it means to enter the border of another country and fight alongside bandits." Go to BBCAfrica.com , external for more news from the African continent. ethiopia.title: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
ethiopia.content: Ethiopian conflict: TPLF forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital Mekelle - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital Image source, Getty Images Image caption, A pro-government soldier standing guard on a street in Ethiopia's Tigray region on Sunday By Teklemariam Bekit , editor, BBC Tigrinya, and Jack Burgess Published 4 October 2026 Updated 5 October 2026 Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city. The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said it decised to leave because of concerns about risks to civilians. Two Mekelle residents told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF fighters have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services had been restored. Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and allied groups and government forces in parts of the northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara. TPLF chairman Debretsion Gebremichael said that while they were leaving Mekelle for the timebeing, the conflict remained fluid and the group would "continue its work from another location". He described it as a deliberate strategic move, saying: "We will attack the enemy where we choose, not where he chooses for us." During the 2020-2022 civil war in Tigray, the TPLF made a similar move and resorted to guerrilla attacks after losing control of Mekelle to federal forces. The latest outbreak of fighting has raised concerns among observers that the conflict could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries. The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours. The presidents of Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan - which all have strained relations with Ethiopia - met on Sunday in the Egyptian coastal city of El-Alamein. They called for "respecting the sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity of states" and the resolution of disputes through "peaceful means". Ethiopia accuses Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan of supporting the Tigray rebels, which they deny. How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia Published 2 October Duke Burbridge, an American doctor with the Health Professionals Network for Tigray, told the BBC that the situation had been calm since the rebels pulled out, except for some outbreaks of gunfire and looting shortly after the withdrawal. He said it "appeared some people who were released from prison or some of the criminal gangs around here [who] were well armed" were involved. Telecommunication services, which had been cut, had now been restored, he said. "[Yesterday] everybody was in the restaurants, in the markets, enjoying the fact that cell phones were back on, mobile banking was back on, and there was loud music deep into the night," he told the BBC Newsday programme. Burbridge said some relative normality was returning, although some food items, including fruits and vegetables, were not available. Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides. However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement. Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power. The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied. Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave. The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need. Ethiopia and Egypt have been embroiled in a longer dispute over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam built on the River Nile, which Cairo fears could reduce its share of water from the river. On Sunday, the four leaders meeting in Egypt affirmed respect sovereignty and non-interference in the internal affairs of the regional states, while calling for adherence to international law over the use of Nile waters. In a joint statement, they rejected "unilateral measures" that could harm downstream countries, in an apparent reference to tensions over Ethiopia's dam. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties as northern conflict escalates
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties as Tigray conflict escalates - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties as northern conflict escalates Image source, Reuters Image caption, More than 50 people have been killed since heavy fighting resumed in northern Ethiopia last week By Wycliffe Muia Published 2 October 2026 Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises fears of a wider regional conflict. On Thursday, Ethiopia announced it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country within 48 hours, accusing them of activities that threatened national security. Eritrea responded by cutting diplomatic relations, saying Ethiopia's decision had left it with no choice but to take reciprocal action. Meanwhile, a pro-government militia says it has seized the town of Milazat, which is just 20km (12 miles) south-east of Mekelle, the capital of Tigray, where the main anti-government group is based. The BBC has not been able to verify this claim. The diplomatic confrontation came hours after powerful explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa , including near Ethiopia's military headquarters. It follows a sharp deterioration in relations between the neighbours, with Ethiopia accusing Eritrea of supporting a new rebel alliance – an allegation Asmara has repeatedly denied. Eritrea described the decision to expel its ambassador as "astounding". "Eritrea has no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia," its foreign ministry said, warning of "negative corollaries" from the decision. The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian federal forces battle fighters from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies across parts of the northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara. Ethiopia has also expelled an Egyptian diplomat, giving him 48 hours to leave the country, according to state media. The government has not publicly given a reason for the decision. Egypt responded by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period, according to the state-affiliated Al Qahera News. Relations between Ethiopia and Egypt have been strained for years, largely over Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), a huge hydroelectric project on the Blue Nile. Egypt, which relies heavily on the Nile for its water supplies, has long expressed concern about the dam's potential impact on its share of the river's water. How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia Published 2 October WATCH: Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? Published 28 September The cutting of ties between Ethiopia and Eritrea mark a dramatic reversal from 2018, when Abiy restored relations with Asmara after two decades of hostility, prompting joyous scenes as the border reopened and families separated for years were reunited. The rapprochement helped earn the Ethiopian prime minister the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019. The latest hostilities are the most serious since a peace agreement ended the devastating Tigray war in 2022. An African Union mediator previously estimated that about 600,000 people had died during that two-year conflict. Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power. A pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers had been involved on the front lines. The BBC has not independently verified the allegation. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and the internet and phone lines have been cut, making it difficult to get reliable information from the region. It is not clear who was responsible for cutting communications. In a rare response to the BBC before diplomatic relations were severed, Eritrea's Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel denied that it was involved in the fighting in Tigray, which borders his country. He told BBC Tigrinya that Ethiopia's governing Prosperity Party was blaming neighbouring countries to divert attention from conflicts and other problems within Ethiopia. The two countries were allies during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF. But relations have deteriorated significantly since then, particularly over Ethiopia's push for direct access to the Red Sea. Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993. Abiy has repeatedly argued that access to the sea is essential to Ethiopia's long-term economic and security interests, while Eritrea has accused his government of harbouring ambitions over its ports. Federal forces and their allies appear to have made gains in southern Tigray and are advancing towards Mekelle, the regional capital. In Alamata, a doctor told the BBC earlier this week that at least 52 civilians had been killed during three days of intense fighting. The TPLF has also been fighting in neighbouring Afar, which lies along Ethiopia's crucial transport corridor to Djibouti and the sea. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to have fled their homes there. Both the Ethiopian government and the TPLF accuse the other of starting the latest hostilities. Tigrayan authorities say their forces were responding to a federal offensive and drone strikes, while Addis Ababa says Tigrayan fighters launched attacks after taking control of federally administered airports in Tigray. The African Union has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise restraint and resolve their differences through diplomatic channels, warning against actions that could further destabilise the region. The UN has also warned that the deteriorating security situation is severely disrupting humanitarian work in northern Ethiopia. UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said drone activity and air strikes were putting civilians, vital infrastructure and aid operations at risk, while insecurity and road closures were restricting humanitarian movements. The UN has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need. ethiopia.title: How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia fighting: Could the conflict between Tigray's TPLF and the army spread? - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia Image source, Reuters Image caption, Tigrayan forces have been patrolling the streets of Tigray's capital, Mekelle, this week By Lucy Fleming and BBC Africa Published 26 September 2026 Updated 2 October 2026 Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army. Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict. There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted. This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago. Why has fighting broken out now? It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray. The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions. This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting. This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation. The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray. Who are the TPLF? For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government. It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades. At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population. When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence. Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century. The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine. An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022. Why has the peace deal faltered? There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray. The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army. Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991. When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa. The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum. Image source, Reuters Image caption, People have been reportedly rushing to buy food, panicking that a full-blown war will start For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms. The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy. But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy. This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions. Who is backing the TPLF? A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies. Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army. Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power. Figure caption, Seven rebel groups from across Ethiopia have announced a new alliance So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside. TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated. Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests. What is the government's position? As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country. It has also accused neighbouring Eritrea of supporting the rebel alliance, something Asmara denies. The row has led the two countries to cut diplomatic ties with each other . During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out. Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports. Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force. What do we know about the bombing in Tigray? Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces. The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify. Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war. This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces. The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks. What is being done to stop the fighting? The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks. It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently. The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict. The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume. The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated. Could the fighting spread? Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia. The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia. The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily. There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government. The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters. The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis. ethiopia.title: Explosions heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned
ethiopia.content: Addis Ababa explosions: Blasts heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Explosions heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, There have been concerns for security in the capital following the outbreak of fighting last week By Lucy Fleming , BBC Africa and Teklemariam Bekit , BBC Tigrinya Published 1 October 2026 Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital, some in the area of the military headquarters in the west and another in the south of the city, residents and diplomatic sources say. The blasts came hours after drone flights were banned over Addis Ababa and a week after fighting erupted in the north between the army and a newly launched alliance of armed groups including forces from the Tigray region. A source linked to the opposition fighters told the Reuters news agency they were behind what they said were drone strikes. "It was very loud. It was strong enough to set off car alarms," a resident in a southern area of the city, near the base of the secret service, told BBC Amharic. He estimated that he heard the explosion in the Gotera neighbourhood some time around 00:30 local time (21:30 GMT). Another resident told the BBC that he and his friends were playing games when they heard an explosion. He lives in the western suburb of Torhayloch, a neighbourhood close to the military headquarters. There were no official reports confirming the cause of the explosions, the exact locations affected or whether there were any casualties or damage. The office of Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, the defence ministry as well as the federal and Addis Ababa police have not responded to BBC requests for comment. Meanwhile, Ethiopia's foreign ministry has said it is closing its embassy in neighbouring Eritrea and expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats "for involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security". Earlier, in a BBC interview, Eritrea's government denied that it was backing the new rebel alliance. Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray? Published 2 October WATCH: Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? Published 28 September Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). They both accuse each other of violating a 2022 peace deal that ended a brutal two-year civil war, which according to an Africa Union mediator is estimated to have cost 600,000 lives. Last month, seven armed movements, including the TPLF and an Amhara militia known as Fano, formed an alliance with the stated aim of removing the government in Addis Ababa. There is disagreement over which side started the latest fighting. The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas. It is difficult to verify what is happening on the ground and access to the internet and the main telecoms service provider in Tigray have also been cut. Within Tigray, the national army and a pro-government militia appear to be advancing towards the region's main city of Mekelle. In the southern Tigrayan town of Alamata, a medic told the BBC on Wednesday that 52 civilians had died in three days of heavy fighting . The TPLF is also reported to be fighting in neighbouring Afar region, a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports. A humanitarian source has estimated that tens of thousands have fled their homes in Afar, according to the AFP news agency. Fighting around Lalibela in the Amhara region, a Unesco world heritage site where foreign tourists have been stranded for more than a week, has involved the national army and Fano fighters, now allied to the TPLF. The government has accused neighbouring Eritrea of backing these groups. One pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers were involved on the front lines. But in a rare response to the BBC from Eritrea's government, Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel dismissed the allegations. He accused Ethiopia's ruling Prosperity Party (PP) of seeking external scapegoats for the country's mounting challenges. "The PP regime has made it a habit to apportion blame to its neighbours in order to deflect attention from the myriad internal conflicts that it is fomenting in various parts of the country," he told BBC Tigrinya. Eritrea was a key ally of Ethiopia during the Tigray war, fighting against the TPLF. But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports. Ethiopia lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Abiy has even hinted at taking the port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - by force as he sees direct access to the sea as important for Ethiopia's long-term future and economic prosperity. As concerns over security mount in Ethiopia, the country's National Intelligence and Security Service (Niss) announced on Wednesday that it was imposing an indefinite ban on drone flights in Addis Ababa and surrounding areas. The agency said it would not issue permits for drone operations and warned that legal action would be taken against anyone flying drones in restricted areas. Niss said the measure was necessary to protect national leaders, critical infrastructure and major public events.
